decks.title: Linear Programming — Part 1: Formulation and feasible regions
goals: Use the terms decision variable, objective function, constraint and non-negativity
Formulate a linear programming problem from a short situation
Draw the half-plane of a linear inequality using a test point
Identify bounded, unbounded and empty feasible regions and list their corner points

slides.heading: Linear Programming, Part 1: Setting up the problem
slides.body_md: Limited flour, limited oven time — how many of each cake earns the most?

visual.alt: Two straight lines in the first quadrant: 2 x plus y equals 40, steep, from (20, 0) up to the y-axis at 40; and 2 x plus 3 y equals 72, gentler, from the y-axis at 24 to the x-axis at 36. They cross at (12, 16). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (20, 0), (12, 16) and (0, 24).
visual.caption: The bakery's feasible region: a quadrilateral with four corners.

slides.narration: Welcome. A bakery has only so much flour and so many oven hours, and two kinds of cake that earn different profits. Which mix of cakes is best? Questions like this, with straight-line limits and a straight-line goal, are linear programming problems. In this part you will learn to write such a problem in symbols and to draw the region of all the plans that are actually possible.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Name the parts of a **linear programming problem** (LPP)
**Formulate** an LPP from a short situation
Draw the region of a linear inequality with a **test point**
Find the **feasible region** and its **corner points**
Recognise **bounded**, **unbounded** and **empty** regions
slides.narration: Here are the goals of part one. First the vocabulary, then the skill of turning words into inequalities. After that we draw half-planes, combine them into a feasible region, and find its corners. Part two will use those corners to find the best plan.

slides.heading: Optimising under limits
slides.body_md: We want the **largest** profit or the **smallest** cost, but every plan must respect **limits** on resources. When the goal and all the limits are **linear**, the problem is a linear programming problem.

visual.alt: Table for the Kanpur bakery: a sponge cake uses 300 grams of flour and 20 minutes of oven time and earns 60 rupees; a fruit cake uses 150 grams and 30 minutes and earns 80 rupees. Available: 6000 grams of flour and 720 minutes.
visual.caption: Turn each row of the table into one line of the problem.

slides.narration: Look at the bakery table. A sponge cake needs three hundred grams of flour and twenty minutes in the oven; a fruit cake needs one hundred and fifty grams and thirty minutes. The baker has six kilograms of flour and twelve hours of oven time, and earns sixty or eighty rupees per cake. Every row of this table will become one line of our problem.

slides.heading: The vocabulary
slides.body_md: Every linear programming problem has the same four parts.

visual.alt: Table of the four basic terms. Decision variables: quantities we choose, here x sponge and y fruit cakes. Objective function: the linear quantity to optimise, here profit 60 x plus 80 y. Constraints: linear limits, here 2 x plus y at most 40 and 2 x plus 3 y at most 72. Non-negativity: x and y at least 0.
visual.caption: The vocabulary of a linear programming problem.

slides.narration: The decision variables are the quantities we are free to choose, here the numbers of each cake. The objective function is the quantity we want to make as large or as small as possible, here the profit. The constraints are the limits, written as linear inequalities. And the non-negativity constraints say we cannot bake a negative number of cakes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: formulate the bakery problem
slides.body_md: Let $x$ sponge cakes and $y$ fruit cakes be baked.
bullets: **Objective:** maximise $Z = 60x + 80y$
**Flour:** $300x + 150y \le 6000 \Rightarrow 2x + y \le 40$
**Oven:** $20x + 30y \le 720 \Rightarrow 2x + 3y \le 72$
**Non-negativity:** $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$

visual.alt: Table testing three bakery plans: (10, 10) gives 30 and 50, feasible; (12, 16) gives exactly 40 and 72, feasible and a corner; (15, 15) gives 45 and 75, breaking both constraints, so infeasible.
visual.caption: A plan is feasible only if it passes every constraint.

slides.narration: Name the variables first, with what they count. The profit is sixty x plus eighty y. Flour used is three hundred x plus one hundred and fifty y, at most six thousand grams; dividing by one hundred and fifty gives two x plus y at most forty. Oven minutes give two x plus three y at most seventy two. The table tests three plans against these constraints.

slides.heading: Graphing one inequality
slides.body_md: The line $2x + 3y = 12$ splits the plane into two **half-planes**. Test a point not on the line, usually the origin: $0 \le 12$ is true, so $2x + 3y \le 12$ is the origin side.

visual.alt: The line 2 x plus 3 y equals 12 through (6, 0) and (0, 4). The origin O lies below the line and P at (4, 3) lies above it. Since 0 is at most 12, the half-plane containing the origin is the solution set of 2 x plus 3 y at most 12.
visual.caption: Test the origin: $0 \le 12$ is true, so shade the origin side.

slides.narration: To draw an inequality, first draw its boundary line using the two intercepts. The line divides the plane into two halves. Pick a test point that is not on the line, usually the origin, and substitute. If the inequality is true there, the origin side is the solution; if false, the other side is. Points on the line itself are included when the sign allows equality.

slides.heading: Quick check: which point fits?
slides.body_md: Substitute each point into the inequality.
slides.narration: Substitute each point carefully and remember that equality is allowed for an at most sign.

slides.heading: The feasible region
slides.body_md: The **feasible region** is the set of points satisfying **all** constraints at once: the overlap of the half-planes, inside the first quadrant. For $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$ it is a quadrilateral.

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 8, through (8, 0) and (0, 8), and x plus 2 y equals 10, through (10, 0) and (0, 5), crossing at (6, 2). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5).
visual.caption: Corners of the region: $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 5)$.

slides.narration: Each constraint gives one half-plane. The non-negativity constraints keep us in the first quadrant. The feasible region is the part of the plane that lies in every one of these half-planes at the same time. Here the two lines cut out a four-sided region below both of them. Any point inside or on its boundary is a feasible plan.

slides.heading: Feasible, infeasible and optimal
slides.body_md: A point of the feasible region is a **feasible solution**; a point outside is **infeasible**. A feasible solution that gives the best value of $Z$ is an **optimal solution**.

visual.alt: Table testing three bakery plans: (10, 10) gives 30 and 50, feasible; (12, 16) gives exactly 40 and 72, feasible and a corner; (15, 15) gives 45 and 75, breaking both constraints, so infeasible.
visual.caption: A plan is feasible only if it passes every constraint.

slides.narration: Three words to keep apart. Feasible means the plan obeys every constraint. Infeasible means it breaks at least one. Optimal means it is feasible and also gives the best possible value of the objective. In the table, ten sponge and ten fruit cakes is feasible but probably not the best, while fifteen of each is not even allowed.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: corners of a region
slides.body_md: Find the corner points of $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: On the axes: $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$ from the first line, $(0, 5)$ from the second
Intersection: subtract the equations, $y = 2$, then $x = 6$
Reject $(10, 0)$ and $(0, 8)$: each breaks the other constraint

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 8, through (8, 0) and (0, 8), and x plus 2 y equals 10, through (10, 0) and (0, 5), crossing at (6, 2). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5).
visual.caption: Corners of the region: $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 5)$.

slides.narration: Corners come from pairs of boundary lines. The axis points are easy; just be sure each one obeys the other constraint. For example zero comma eight lies on the first line but gives sixteen in the second, more than ten, so it is not a corner. The two slanting lines meet where we subtract the equations: y is two and x is six. So the corners are four points.

slides.heading: Quick check: test the origin
slides.body_md: Decide which side of the line to shade.
slides.narration: Put zero for both variables and ask whether the inequality is then true or false.

slides.heading: Bounded and unbounded regions
slides.body_md: A region that fits inside some circle is **bounded**. The region $x + y \ge 6$, $x + 3y \ge 9$, $x, y \ge 0$ stretches without end: it is **unbounded**, but it still has corners.

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 6 and x plus 3 y equals 9, crossing at (4.5, 1.5). The feasible region lies above and to the right of both lines and stretches without end: it is unbounded, with corners (0, 6), (4.5, 1.5) and (9, 0).
visual.caption: An unbounded region: the corners exist, but the region has no far edge.

slides.narration: Some regions are closed off on every side, like the quadrilateral we just found; they are bounded. Others run away to infinity. Here both constraints say at least, so every point far enough out is feasible. The region still has three corners, but it has no far edge, and that will matter when we look for a maximum.

slides.heading: Finding a corner algebraically
slides.body_md: Every corner is the meeting point of **two** boundary lines (the axes count). Solve the pair, then **check** the point in every other constraint.

visual.alt: Table of the corners of the unbounded region with the pair of lines that make each: (0, 6) from x equals 0 and x plus y equals 6; (4.5, 1.5) from x plus y equals 6 and x plus 3 y equals 9; (9, 0) from y equals 0 and x plus 3 y equals 9.
visual.caption: Each corner and the two lines that make it.

slides.narration: Do not read corners off a rough sketch. Pick the two boundary lines that meet there, solve them as simultaneous equations, and then check the point in every other constraint. A crossing point that breaks some other constraint is outside the region and is not a corner.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an "at least" constraint
slides.body_md: A spice exporter in Kochi packs $x$ boxes of pepper and $y$ of cardamom per day. The sealing machine can handle at most $50$ boxes, and an order needs at least $40$ "points", where a pepper box counts $2$ and a cardamom box $1$.
bullets: Machine: $x + y \le 50$
Order: $2x + y \ge 40$
$x, y \ge 0$

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 50 and 2 x plus y equals 40. The first keeps points on the origin side, the second keeps points away from the origin. The feasible region is the four-sided strip between them with corners (0, 40), (20, 0), (50, 0) and (0, 50).
visual.caption: A region between two lines: one "at most" and one "at least" constraint.

slides.narration: Words like at most give a less than or equal sign; words like at least give a greater than or equal sign. Here the machine limit keeps us below one line, and the order keeps us above another. The feasible region is the strip between them. Test points help: ten and ten gives only thirty points, so it fails the order.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the region
slides.body_md: Recall the vocabulary.
slides.narration: Think about the set of all points that obey every one of the constraints together.

slides.heading: When there is no feasible region
slides.body_md: $x + y \le 3$ and $2x + 3y \ge 12$ (with $x, y \ge 0$) have **no common point**: the region is **empty** and the problem has **no solution**.

visual.alt: Two lines in the first quadrant: x plus y equals 3 from (3, 0) to (0, 3), and 2 x plus 3 y equals 12 from (6, 0) to (0, 4). The first constraint keeps points below the lower line, the second keeps points above the upper line, so no point satisfies both.
visual.caption: No overlap: the feasible region is empty.

slides.narration: Sometimes the constraints contradict each other. The first keeps us below the lower line, the second above the upper line, and these two zones never overlap in the first quadrant. Then there is no feasible plan at all, so there is nothing to optimise. In an exam, say clearly that the feasible region is empty.

slides.heading: Quick check: is the point feasible?
slides.body_md: Test the point in every constraint.
slides.narration: Substitute the point into both inequalities, and remember the non negativity conditions too.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: An LPP has decision variables, a linear **objective**, linear **constraints** and **non-negativity**
Each inequality is a **half-plane**; use a test point to choose the side
The **feasible region** is the common part of all the half-planes
**Corners** come from pairs of boundary lines, checked in every constraint
Regions can be **bounded**, **unbounded** or **empty**

rows: Max and min both exist, at corners
An optimum may or may not exist
Equal best values at adjacent corners

visual.alt: Summary table of the cases: a bounded non-empty region always has a maximum and a minimum at corners; an unbounded region may or may not have an optimum, decided by the half-plane test; two tied adjacent corners give infinitely many optimal points; an empty region means no solution.
visual.caption: Four situations every student should recognise.

slides.narration: To sum up. Write the variables, the objective and every constraint, including non negativity. Draw each boundary line and shade with a test point. The overlap is the feasible region. Find its corners by solving pairs of lines. And notice whether the region is bounded, unbounded or empty, because that decides what can happen next.

slides.heading: Exam tips for formulation and regions
bullets: Define each variable with its **unit** ("$x$ = number of sponge cakes per day")
Write constraints in **simplest form**; keep the same units on both sides
Label every line with its **equation** and mark its intercepts
Show the **test point** used for shading
List all corners, including those on the axes, with **coordinates**
The deleted "types of LPP" classification is **not** in the 2026–27 syllabus

Label every line and its intercepts on the graph, mention your test point, and write every corner with its coordinates. Classifying problems into named types is not in this year's syllabus, so spend your time on formulation and graphs.

decks.title: Linear Programming — Part 2: The corner-point method
goals: State the Corner Point Theorem for bounded regions
Solve two-variable linear programming problems by the corner-point method
Use the half-plane test on unbounded regions
Recognise multiple optimal solutions and problems with no solution

slides.heading: Linear Programming, Part 2: The corner-point method
slides.body_md: The best plan always sits at a corner — if a best plan exists.

visual.alt: The quadrilateral region with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5), and two parallel objective lines 3 x plus 5 y equals 15 and 3 x plus 5 y equals 28. Sliding the line outwards, the last point of the region it touches is the corner (6, 2).
visual.caption: Parallel lines $3x + 5y = k$: the last region point touched is a corner.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. We have feasible regions and their corners. Now we find the best plan. Picture lines of equal profit, all parallel, sliding across the region. The last point of the region they touch is always a corner. That simple picture is the heart of the corner point method.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: State the **Corner Point Theorem**
Solve LPPs with the **corner-point method**
Apply the **half-plane test** on unbounded regions
Recognise **multiple optimal solutions**
Recognise problems with **no** solution
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part two. By the end you will solve any two variable problem in your syllabus: bounded or unbounded regions, a unique best plan, a whole edge of best plans, or no best plan at all.

slides.heading: Corner Point Theorem
slides.body_md: If the feasible region is **bounded** (and non-empty), $Z = ax + by$ has **both** a maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a **corner point**. If the region is **unbounded**, an optimum, **if it exists**, also occurs at a corner.

visual.alt: The quadrilateral region with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5), and two parallel objective lines 3 x plus 5 y equals 15 and 3 x plus 5 y equals 28. Sliding the line outwards, the last point of the region it touches is the corner (6, 2).
visual.caption: Parallel lines $3x + 5y = k$: the last region point touched is a corner.

slides.narration: Here is the key result. The objective lines are parallel. As you slide one across a bounded region, the value of the objective grows steadily, and the last region point the line touches is a corner. So on a bounded region the maximum and the minimum both exist and both sit at corners. On an unbounded region an optimum may fail to exist, but if it exists it is still at a corner.

slides.heading: The corner-point method
slides.body_md: Six steps, every time.

Find every corner (solve pairs of lines)
Evaluate $Z$ at each corner
Bounded: largest/smallest corner value is the answer
Unbounded: half-plane test before accepting

visual.alt: Flow chart of the corner-point method: formulate, draw the boundary lines and shade, identify the feasible region, find every corner, evaluate Z at each corner; if the region is bounded, the largest or smallest value is the answer; if unbounded, apply the half-plane test first.
visual.caption: The corner-point method in six steps.

slides.narration: Formulate the problem. Draw each boundary line and shade with a test point. Identify the feasible region. Find every corner by solving pairs of lines. Evaluate the objective at each corner. If the region is bounded, read off the largest or smallest value. If it is unbounded, carry out one more check, the half plane test, before you accept the answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: maximise on a bounded region
slides.body_md: Maximise $Z = 3x + 5y$ subject to $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: Bounded region: maximum $28$ at $x = 6$, $y = 2$

visual.alt: Corner table for Z equals 3 x plus 5 y: (0, 0) gives 0, (8, 0) gives 24, (6, 2) gives 28, the maximum, and (0, 5) gives 25.
visual.caption: Largest corner value: $28$ at $(6, 2)$.

slides.narration: We already know the corners of this region. Put each into three x plus five y. Zero, twenty four, twenty eight and twenty five. The region is bounded, so the largest of these, twenty eight, is the maximum, at x equals six and y equals two. Notice that the best corner is not on an axis: it is where both resources run out together.

slides.heading: The minimum comes for free
slides.body_md: On the same bounded region the **minimum** of $Z = 3x + 5y$ is the smallest corner value: $0$ at $(0, 0)$. One table answers both questions.

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 8, through (8, 0) and (0, 8), and x plus 2 y equals 10, through (10, 0) and (0, 5), crossing at (6, 2). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5).
visual.caption: Corners of the region: $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 5)$.

slides.narration: Once you have the table of corner values on a bounded region, both answers are in front of you. The smallest value, zero, is the minimum, at the origin. In real problems the minimum of a profit is rarely interesting, but for cost problems it is exactly what we want, and the regions then usually do not contain the origin.

slides.heading: Quick check: where do two lines meet?
slides.body_md: Solve the two boundary equations together.
slides.narration: Subtract one equation from the other to remove a variable, then substitute back.

slides.heading: Unbounded regions need one more step
slides.body_md: On an unbounded region the best corner value is only a **candidate**. Test the open half-plane beyond it.

nodes.label: Smallest corner value $m$ (or largest $M$)
Draw $ax + by = m$; look at the open half-plane $ax + by < m$ (or $> M$)
Does it share any point with the region?
No: $m$ is the minimum (or $M$ the maximum)
Yes: no minimum (or no maximum)

visual.alt: Flow chart of the half-plane test for an unbounded region: take the smallest corner value m, draw the line a x plus b y equals m, and look at the open half-plane a x plus b y less than m. If it shares no point with the region, m is the minimum; otherwise there is no minimum. The same works for a maximum with greater than M.
visual.caption: The extra step for unbounded regions.

slides.narration: Why the extra step? On an unbounded region, the objective might keep improving forever as we move out. So the smallest corner value, call it m, is only a candidate. Draw the line where the objective equals m and look at the open half plane where it is smaller. If that half plane shares no point with the region, m really is the minimum. If it does, there is no minimum.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a minimum on an unbounded region
slides.body_md: Minimise $Z = 2x + 3y$ subject to $x + y \ge 6$, $x + 3y \ge 9$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: Draw $2x + 3y = 13.5$: the half-plane $2x + 3y < 13.5$ has **no** point of the region

visual.alt: The unbounded region above x plus y equals 6 and x plus 3 y equals 9, with the dashed objective line 2 x plus 3 y equals 13.5 touching it only at the corner (4.5, 1.5). Every other point of the region lies on the far side of this line.
visual.caption: The half-plane $2x + 3y < 13.5$ misses the region, so the minimum is $13.5$.

slides.narration: The corners of this unbounded region give eighteen, thirteen point five and eighteen. The candidate minimum is thirteen point five. Now draw the line two x plus three y equals thirteen point five. It touches the region only at the corner, and the whole region lies on the far side. So the open half plane of smaller values misses the region, and thirteen point five is the minimum.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: no maximum
slides.body_md: On the same region, maximise $Z = x + y$.
bullets: Corner values: $6$, $6$, $9$; largest $9$
Half-plane $x + y > 9$: the point $(20, 20)$ is feasible and gives $40$
The half-plane meets the region, so $Z$ has **no maximum**

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 6 and x plus 3 y equals 9, crossing at (4.5, 1.5). The feasible region lies above and to the right of both lines and stretches without end: it is unbounded, with corners (0, 6), (4.5, 1.5) and (9, 0).
visual.caption: An unbounded region: the corners exist, but the region has no far edge.

slides.narration: Now try to maximise x plus y on the same region. The corners give six, six and nine. But the region runs away to infinity, and a feasible point like twenty comma twenty gives forty, far more than nine. The half plane where x plus y exceeds nine meets the region, so there is no maximum value at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: how many best points?
slides.body_md: Two corners tie for the best value.
slides.narration: Work out the objective at every corner and look for a tie between neighbouring corners.

slides.heading: Multiple optimal solutions
slides.body_md: If $Z$ takes the same best value at **two adjacent corners**, it takes that value along the **whole edge** joining them: infinitely many optimal solutions.

visual.alt: The quadrilateral region with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5). The objective line 2 x plus 4 y equals 20 lies exactly along the edge from (0, 5) to (6, 2), so it touches the region along a whole edge.
visual.caption: Objective parallel to an edge: every point of that edge is optimal.

slides.narration: Sometimes the objective lines are parallel to one edge of the region. Then, as the line slides out, it leaves the region along a whole edge rather than a single corner. Both end corners give the same best value, and so does every point in between. We say the problem has infinitely many optimal solutions.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an edge of optimal points
slides.body_md: Maximise $Z = 2x + 4y$ on $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: Maximum $20$ at both $(6, 2)$ and $(0, 5)$
So every point of the segment joining them is optimal, e.g. $(3, 3.5)$ gives $6 + 14 = 20$

visual.alt: Corner table for Z equals 2 x plus 4 y: (0, 0) gives 0, (8, 0) gives 16, and both (6, 2) and (0, 5) give the maximum 20.
visual.caption: Tie at two adjacent corners: the whole edge is optimal.

slides.narration: Here two x plus four y is just twice the boundary expression x plus two y. At the corners we get zero, sixteen, twenty and twenty. The maximum, twenty, appears at two neighbouring corners, so it holds all along the edge between them. The midpoint three comma three point five also gives twenty. Write this conclusion in words in your answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the bakery, solved
slides.body_md: Maximise $Z = 60x + 80y$ subject to $2x + y \le 40$, $2x + 3y \le 72$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: Intersection: subtract, $2y = 32$, $y = 16$, $x = 12$
Bake $12$ sponge and $16$ fruit cakes: profit ₹$2000$

visual.alt: Two straight lines in the first quadrant: 2 x plus y equals 40, steep, from (20, 0) up to the y-axis at 40; and 2 x plus 3 y equals 72, gentler, from the y-axis at 24 to the x-axis at 36. They cross at (12, 16). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (20, 0), (12, 16) and (0, 24).
visual.caption: The bakery's feasible region: a quadrilateral with four corners.

slides.narration: Back to the bakery. Subtract the constraint equations to get y equals sixteen, then x equals twelve. The four corners give profits of zero, twelve hundred, two thousand and nineteen hundred and twenty rupees. The region is bounded, so the best plan is twelve sponge cakes and sixteen fruit cakes, for a profit of two thousand rupees. Always end with the answer in words.

slides.heading: Quick check: a candidate on an unbounded region
slides.body_md: Decide whether a minimum can exist.
slides.narration: Remember that an unbounded region can still have a smallest value, if the half plane test is passed.

slides.heading: Mistakes that cost marks
slides.body_md: Most errors are not in the arithmetic but in the method.

Keeping a crossing point outside the region

Accepting the best corner on an unbounded region

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes and fixes: missing an axis corner, check every line against both axes; keeping a crossing point outside the region, test each corner; accepting the best corner on an unbounded region, do the half-plane test; stating one point when corners tie, state the whole edge; shading the wrong side, use a test point.
visual.caption: Five habits that protect your marks.

slides.narration: Here are the five commonest mistakes. Missing a corner on an axis. Keeping a crossing point that breaks another constraint. Forgetting the half plane test on an unbounded region. Naming only one point when two corners tie. And shading the wrong side of a line. Each has a simple fix, shown in the table.

slides.body_md: Evaluate the objective at each corner.
slides.narration: Substitute each corner into the objective and take the largest value.

notes.title: Linear Programming — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. What is a linear programming problem?
sections.body_md:
A **linear programming problem** (LPP) asks for the maximum or minimum of a **linear objective function** $Z = ax + by$ when the variables must satisfy **linear constraints** (inequalities) and the **non-negativity constraints** $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$.

The variables $x$ and $y$ are the **decision variables**: the quantities we choose (numbers of items, hours, kilograms).

key_terms.definition_md: The unknown quantities to be chosen.
The linear function $Z = ax + by$ to be maximised or minimised.
Linear inequalities that every plan must satisfy.

formulas.latex: \text{Optimise } Z = ax + by \text{ subject to } a_ix + b_iy \le c_i \text{ (or } \ge c_i\text{)},\ x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0
formulas.label: General form (two variables)

visual.alt: Table of the four basic terms. Decision variables: quantities we choose, here x sponge and y fruit cakes. Objective function: the linear quantity to optimise, here profit 60 x plus 80 y. Constraints: linear limits, here 2 x plus y at most 40 and 2 x plus 3 y at most 72. Non-negativity: x and y at least 0.
visual.caption: The vocabulary of a linear programming problem.

sections.heading: 2. Formulating a problem
sections.body_md:
**Steps:** (1) define the decision variables with units; (2) write the objective function; (3) write one constraint for each limited resource or requirement; (4) add non-negativity.

**Translations:** "at most", "cannot exceed", "available" give $\le$; "at least", "must meet" give $\ge$. Simplify each constraint by dividing by a common factor, and keep units the same on both sides.

Example (Kanpur bakery): $x$ sponge, $y$ fruit cakes; maximise $Z = 60x + 80y$ subject to $2x + y \le 40$ (flour), $2x + 3y \le 72$ (oven), $x, y \ge 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: Writing a situation as an objective and constraints.

visual.alt: Table for the Kanpur bakery: a sponge cake uses 300 grams of flour and 20 minutes of oven time and earns 60 rupees; a fruit cake uses 150 grams and 30 minutes and earns 80 rupees. Available: 6000 grams of flour and 720 minutes.
visual.caption: Turn each row of the table into one line of the problem.

sections.heading: 3. Graphing linear inequalities
sections.body_md:
The line $ax + by = c$ divides the plane into two **half-planes**. To decide which side satisfies $ax + by \le c$, substitute a **test point** not on the line (the origin if possible): if the inequality is true there, that side is the solution set.

Draw the line using its intercepts. Points on the line belong to the region for $\le$ and $\ge$.

key_terms.definition_md: One of the two parts into which a line divides the plane.
A point not on the line, substituted to choose the side.

formulas.latex: \text{intercepts of } ax + by = c:\ \left(\dfrac ca, 0\right),\ \left(0, \dfrac cb\right)
formulas.label: Drawing the line

visual.alt: The line 2 x plus 3 y equals 12 through (6, 0) and (0, 4). The origin O lies below the line and P at (4, 3) lies above it. Since 0 is at most 12, the half-plane containing the origin is the solution set of 2 x plus 3 y at most 12.
visual.caption: Test the origin: $0 \le 12$ is true, so shade the origin side.

sections.heading: 4. Feasible region and corner points
sections.body_md:
The **feasible region** is the common part of all the half-planes (including $x, y \ge 0$). Its points are **feasible solutions**; points outside are **infeasible**. An **optimal solution** is a feasible point giving the best value of $Z$.

A **corner point** is a vertex of the region: the meeting point of two boundary lines (or a line and an axis) that satisfies every constraint. Example: $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$ has corners $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 5)$.

A region is **bounded** if it can be enclosed in a circle, otherwise **unbounded**. It may also be **empty**.

key_terms.definition_md: Set of points satisfying all constraints.
A region that can be enclosed in a circle.

visual.alt: The lines x plus y equals 8, through (8, 0) and (0, 8), and x plus 2 y equals 10, through (10, 0) and (0, 5), crossing at (6, 2). The feasible region is the quadrilateral below both lines with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5).
visual.caption: Corners of the region: $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 5)$.

sections.heading: 5. The corner-point method (bounded regions)
sections.body_md:
**Corner Point Theorem.** If the feasible region is bounded and non-empty, $Z = ax + by$ has a maximum and a minimum, both at corner points.

**Method:** draw the region, find all corners, evaluate $Z$ at each, and pick the largest (maximum) or smallest (minimum).

Example: maximise $Z = 3x + 5y$ on the region of section 4: values $0$, $24$, $28$, $25$, so the maximum is $28$ at $(6, 2)$. Bakery: maximum ₹$2000$ at $(12, 16)$.

key_terms.definition_md: On a bounded region, the optimum of a linear objective is at a corner.

sections.heading: 6. Unbounded regions: the half-plane test
sections.body_md:
On an **unbounded** region an optimum may not exist. If an optimum exists, it is at a corner.

**Test for a minimum:** let $m$ be the smallest corner value. If the open half-plane $ax + by < m$ has **no** point in common with the region, $m$ is the minimum; otherwise there is no minimum.

**Test for a maximum:** with $M$ the largest corner value, check $ax + by > M$ in the same way.

Example: on $x + y \ge 6$, $x + 3y \ge 9$, $x, y \ge 0$, $Z = 2x + 3y$ has minimum $13.5$ at $(4.5, 1.5)$, but $Z = x + y$ has no maximum.

key_terms.definition_md: A region that cannot be enclosed in a circle.
Check whether $ax + by < m$ (or $> M$) meets the region.

visual.caption: The half-plane $2x + 3y < 13.5$ misses the region, so the minimum is $13.5$.

sections.heading: 7. Special cases
sections.body_md:
- **Multiple optimal solutions:** if $Z$ has the same best value at two adjacent corners, every point of the edge joining them is optimal (the objective lines are parallel to that edge). Example: $Z = 2x + 4y$ on the region of section 4 is $20$ at $(6, 2)$ and $(0, 5)$.
- **Empty region (infeasible problem):** constraints such as $x + y \le 3$ and $2x + 3y \ge 12$ (with $x, y \ge 0$) have no common point; there is no solution.
- **No optimum:** on an unbounded region the objective may grow (or fall) without limit.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* classifying LPPs into named types (manufacturing, diet, transportation problems).

key_terms.definition_md: Infinitely many optimal points along an edge.
A problem whose feasible region is empty.

visual.alt: The quadrilateral region with corners (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 2) and (0, 5). The objective line 2 x plus 4 y equals 20 lies exactly along the edge from (0, 5) to (6, 2), so it touches the region along a whole edge.
visual.caption: Objective parallel to an edge: every point of that edge is optimal.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Formulation (2–3 marks):* variables defined with units, objective, each constraint, non-negativity.
- *Graphical solution (3–5 marks):* lines with intercepts, correct region, all corners with coordinates, corner table, conclusion in words.
- *Unbounded region:* one mark is usually for the half-plane check (draw $Z = m$ and state the result).
- *Objective (1 mark):* corner values, best corner, feasibility of a point, number of corners.

**Common mistakes**
1. Forgetting the non-negativity constraints, or a corner on an axis.
2. Shading the wrong side of a line (no test point).
3. Mixing units in a constraint (grams with kilograms, minutes with hours).
4. Listing a crossing point that breaks another constraint as a corner.
5. Accepting the best corner on an unbounded region without the half-plane test.
6. Naming one optimal point when two adjacent corners tie.
7. Writing the optimal value but not the plan (or the plan without the value).
8. Reading corners from a rough sketch instead of solving the equations.

questions.stem_md: In a linear programming problem, the objective function is

options.text_md: a linear function of the decision variables that is to be maximised or minimised
any one of the constraints written as an equation
the set of all points satisfying the constraints
a quadratic expression in the decision variables

questions.solution_md: The objective function $Z = ax + by$ is the linear quantity (profit, cost, time) we optimise. Option (c) describes the feasible region, not the objective.

questions.stem_md: Why are the conditions $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ included in almost every linear programming problem drawn from real life?

options.text_md: They make the optimal solution unique
Quantities such as numbers of items, hours or kilograms cannot be negative
They make the objective function linear
They guarantee that the feasible region is bounded

questions.solution_md: These are the non-negativity constraints: decision variables count or measure real things. They do not by themselves make the region bounded or the optimum unique.

questions.stem_md: Which of these points satisfies the inequality $2x + 3y \le 12$?
questions.solution_md: Substitute: $(3, 2)$ gives $6 + 6 = 12$, which is allowed because the inequality includes equality. The others give $14$, $13$ and $14$.

questions.stem_md: The feasible region of $x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 10$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ is a quadrilateral. Which of the following is **not** one of its corner points?
questions.solution_md: $(0, 8)$ lies on $x + y = 8$ but gives $0 + 16 = 16 > 10$, so it breaks the second constraint. The corners are $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, $(6, 2)$ and $(0, 5)$.

questions.stem_md: A bounded feasible region has corner points $(0, 0)$, $(6, 0)$, $(4, 3)$ and $(0, 5)$. The maximum value of $Z = 3x + 4y$ on it is
questions.solution_md: Corner values: $0$, $18$, $24$, $20$. The largest is $24$ at $(4, 3)$. Option (b) is the value at $(0, 5)$ only.

questions.stem_md: For the constraints $x + y \ge 4$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, the feasible region is

options.text_md: a single point
unbounded
a triangle
empty

questions.solution_md: Every point beyond the line $x + y = 4$ in the first quadrant is feasible, for example $(100, 100)$, so the region stretches without end: it is unbounded.

questions.stem_md: The unbounded region defined by $2x + y \ge 8$, $x + 2y \ge 7$, $x, y \ge 0$ has corners $(0, 8)$, $(3, 2)$ and $(7, 0)$. For $Z = 6x + 4y$, the least value on this region is

options.text_md: not attained, as the region is unbounded

questions.solution_md: Corner values: $32$, $26$, $42$. The smallest is $26$; because the region is unbounded, check that $6x + 4y < 26$ has no point in common with it — it has none, so the minimum is $26$ at $(3, 2)$.

questions.stem_md: If the feasible region of a linear programming problem is bounded and non-empty, then the objective function

options.text_md: has a maximum but may have no minimum
has its optimum only at an interior point
may have neither a maximum nor a minimum
has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner point

questions.solution_md: Corner Point Theorem: on a bounded (and non-empty) feasible region, $Z = ax + by$ attains both a maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a corner point.

questions.stem_md: An objective function takes the same maximum value at two adjacent corner points of a bounded feasible region. Then the maximum occurs

options.text_md: at every point of the edge joining those two corners
only at those two corner points
at no point, since the optimum must be unique
only at the midpoint of the edge joining them

questions.solution_md: $Z$ is linear, so along the edge it changes uniformly; equal values at both ends mean it is constant on the whole edge. There are infinitely many optimal solutions.

questions.stem_md: How many corner points does the feasible region of $x + y \ge 2$, $x \le 4$, $y \le 3$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ have?
questions.solution_md: The corners are $(2, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(4, 3)$, $(0, 3)$ and $(0, 2)$: a pentagon, so $5$ corners. The origin is cut away by $x + y \ge 2$.

questions.stem_md: The boundary lines $2x + y = 10$ and $x + y = 7$ meet at a corner of a feasible region. That corner is
questions.solution_md: Subtract: $x = 3$; then $y = 7 - 3 = 4$. Check: $6 + 4 = 10$. Option (d) swaps the coordinates.

questions.stem_md: A baker in Kanpur uses $300$ g of flour for each sponge cake and $150$ g for each fruit cake, and has $6$ kg of flour for the day. With $x$ sponge cakes and $y$ fruit cakes, the flour constraint is
questions.solution_md: Flour used: $300x + 150y \le 6000$ (grams). Dividing by $150$: $2x + y \le 40$. Option (c) mixes grams with kilograms.

questions.stem_md: Consider the constraints $x + y \le 3$, $2x + 3y \ge 12$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: There is no feasible region, so the problem has no solution
The feasible region is unbounded
The only feasible point is $(0, 3)$
The feasible region is a triangle

questions.solution_md: On $x + y \le 3$ in the first quadrant, $2x + 3y$ is at most $9$ (at $(0, 3)$), which is less than $12$. No point satisfies both, so the region is empty. At $(0, 3)$, $2x + 3y$ is only $9$.

questions.stem_md: On the region with corners $(0, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(3, 4)$, $(0, 5)$, the function $Z = 4x + 2y$ is maximised. The number of optimal solutions is

options.text_md: none
infinitely many
exactly one
exactly two

questions.solution_md: $Z(5, 0) = 20$ and $Z(3, 4) = 20$ are equal and largest, so every point of the edge joining them is optimal: infinitely many solutions.

questions.stem_md: A feasible region is unbounded with corners $(0, 8)$, $(3, 2)$, $(7, 0)$ and comes from $2x + y \ge 8$, $x + 2y \ge 7$, $x, y \ge 0$. The minimum of $Z = 3x + 5y$ is

options.text_md: not attained

questions.solution_md: Corner values: $40$, $19$, $21$. Smallest: $19$. The open half-plane $3x + 5y < 19$ has no point of the region, so the minimum is $19$ at $(3, 2)$.

Because of the non-negativity constraints, the feasible region of a two-variable linear programming problem always lies in

options.text_md: the first quadrant (including the axes)
the second quadrant
the half-plane above the x-axis only
the region between the two axes and the origin only

questions.solution_md: $x \ge 0$ keeps points to the right of (or on) the y-axis and $y \ge 0$ keeps them above (or on) the x-axis: together, the first quadrant with its boundary.

$0 \ge 6$ is false, so shade the side of the line away from the origin
$0 \ge 6$ is false, so shade the side containing the origin

options.text_md: True

options.text_md: True

questions.solution_md: False. All constraints and the objective must be **linear** in the decision variables; $xy$ is a product of the variables, so it is not linear.

questions.stem_md: The common region determined by all the constraints, including the non-negativity constraints, is called the ____ region.

answer.model_answer_md:
Corners $(0, 6)$, $(4.5, 1.5)$, $(9, 0)$ give $Z = 18$, $13.5$, $18$. Smallest: $13.5$.
